opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the difference between shorter and longer timelines actually comes down to how much algorithmic progress you're getting and, importantly, whether that progress keeps pace once you start running out of easy compute scaling.

In the shorter-timelines world, the story is roughly: we're getting something like a few-x per year in effective compute from algorithmic improvements, on top of the hardware and spending scale-up. And critically, at some point AIs themselves start meaningfully accelerating AI research. Once you have systems that can do a large fraction of what research engineers do, you might get a big multiplier on the rate of algorithmic progress, because you can throw a huge number of AI researcher-equivalents at the problem. So in that world, algorithmic efficiency isn't just a steady trend; it potentially speeds up, and you get a kind of feedback loop where better algorithms produce better AI researchers, which produce better algorithms.

In the longer-timelines world, I think a few things are different. One is that compute scaling slows down. We're spending a really big fraction of what's feasible already, and there are limits on how fast you can grow fabs, power, and investment. If we don't hit very capable systems by around the end of the decade, the compute growth rate probably drops a lot. Then you're much more reliant on algorithmic progress alone, and the question becomes: how much of past algorithmic progress was actually driven by compute? There's a decent argument that a lot of algorithmic improvement comes from having more compute to run experiments and from ideas that only work at scale. If that's right, then when compute growth slows, algorithmic progress slows too, and you get a sort of double slowdown.

So in the long-timelines world, I'd expect algorithmic efficiency gains per year to be lower, partly because the low-hanging fruit gets picked and partly because experimental compute isn't growing as fast. And you also don't get the AI-accelerated research kick in, or it kicks in much later and more weakly.

The other thing I'd note is that there's a lot of uncertainty about how much of the "algorithmic progress" we measure is really general efficiency versus things like better data, better post-training, RL on specific tasks, and so on. In shorter timelines, a lot of the action might be in things like RL scaling and getting models to do longer-horizon agentic tasks, where the gains could be quite rapid. In longer timelines, maybe those approaches hit diminishing returns and you need some more fundamental insight, which is slower and harder to predict.

So overall, I'd say: short timelines roughly correspond to worlds where algorithmic progress stays fast or accelerates, especially via AI automating AI R&D; long timelines correspond to worlds where it slows down alongside compute, and we have to wait for more fundamental breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response says shorter timelines involve faster or accelerating algorithmic progress, while longer timelines involve lower annual efficiency gains and slower progress, communicating the stated comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about this is that algorithmic progress matters a lot more in the short-timelines worlds than in the long-timelines worlds, and the reason is kind of structural.

So if you look at where the gains have been coming from over the last several years, you've got compute scaling, you've got algorithmic improvements, and then you've got this kind of ramp-up in investment that's been letting people buy way more compute. And the compute side has been growing something like 4x or 5x per year, but a lot of that is because we've been scaling up the fraction of the economy that goes into AI. That can't go on forever. At some point you hit the limits of how much people are willing to spend, how many fabs there are, how much power you can get, and the compute growth rate has to slow down to something more like the underlying hardware improvement rate, which is more like 1.3x or 1.5x a year.

So in the short-timelines world, the picture is basically: we get to really powerful AI before that slowdown kicks in. Maybe it's 2027, 2028, something like that. And in that world, the relevant question about algorithmic efficiency is really just: how much more can you squeeze out of the current paradigm? Do the current trends in training efficiency and inference efficiency keep going at roughly the rate they've been going, and is that enough, combined with another couple of orders of magnitude of compute, to get you to systems that can automate AI research? And I think the answer there is plausibly yes, but it's pretty contingent on the trends holding up.

And then the thing that happens in that world which is really important is that once you have AI that can substantially automate the research process, algorithmic progress itself speeds up. You go from having, I don't know, a few thousand really good researchers at the frontier labs to having effectively millions of them running at many times human speed. And at that point, the algorithmic efficiency gains could be enormous, because you're no longer bottlenecked on human labor; you're bottlenecked on compute for experiments, and even that you can get around to some degree by being smarter about which experiments to run.

In the longer-timelines world, I think the story is kind of the opposite. If we don't get there by around 2030 or so, then I think progress slows down, because the compute scaling has to slow, and algorithmic progress on its own, at the historical rate, just isn't fast enough to get you there quickly. Historically, maybe you get something like 2x or 3x effective compute per year from algorithms. That's a lot, but if you need, say, three or four orders of magnitude more effective compute and you're only getting it from algorithms, that's a decade or more.

So I think in the long-timelines world, you'd probably need some kind of new paradigm or some kind of fundamental insight, something that isn't just continuous improvement on the current recipe. And that's inherently much harder to forecast. Those sorts of things can happen at any time, or they can take 20 years.

The other thing I'd say is that the longer-timelines worlds are also ones where it's more likely that there's some fundamental limit we're running into, like the current approach just doesn't generalize in the ways we'd need, and algorithmic efficiency improvements in the narrow sense don't really address that. You can make the model you have cheaper, but that's different from making it qualitatively more capable.

So to summarize: short timelines are worlds where the current trends continue and then get massively amplified by AI automating research. Long timelines are worlds where those trends slow down or hit a wall and you need something new. And I'd put maybe 25% or so on the short-timelines picture, something like powerful AI by the end of the decade, but with a lot of uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short timelines, where current algorithmic-efficiency trends continue and are amplified by AI research automation, with long timelines, where those gains slow or hit a wall. This communicates that short timelines assume greater algorithmic efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how much time there is for algorithmic improvements to accumulate. On shorter timelines, you’re relying more on scaling up approaches that already work: more compute, bigger training runs, and improvements that are fairly close to what we know how to do today. There can still be substantial efficiency gains, but there’s less time for those to compound.

On longer timelines, there’s more opportunity to find ways to get the same capabilities with less compute. So even if progress in hardware or investment slows down, that doesn’t necessarily imply a comparable slowdown in capabilities. We might just become much better at using the compute we have.

One complication is that AI itself could accelerate algorithmic research. If systems become useful enough at doing that research, you could get a lot of algorithmic progress in a short amount of calendar time. So I wouldn’t treat short timelines as necessarily implying small efficiency gains. It depends on whether we’re talking about improvements made by human researchers at roughly the current pace, or improvements in a world where AI is doing a substantial fraction of the research.

r001.rationale: The response says longer timelines allow more time for algorithmic efficiency gains to accumulate. It notes AI could accelerate research even on short timelines, but does not state that shorter timelines implicitly assume more efficient algorithms than longer ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difference is how much time there is for algorithmic progress to accumulate. If timelines are very short, then a lot of the improvement probably has to come from scaling up methods that are already fairly close to what we have. You can still get substantial efficiency gains, but there’s less time to discover and develop fundamentally different approaches.

If timelines are longer, there’s more room for algorithms to improve, so the amount of compute needed to reach a given capability could be much lower. That also makes it harder to infer when we’ll get powerful AI just by looking at how much compute companies are going to have.

But these aren’t independent variables. If algorithmic progress is faster than we expect, that itself tends to shorten timelines. So I’d distinguish between longer timelines because progress is slow and longer timelines because the problem turns out to require much more computation. Those imply pretty different things about how much algorithmic improvement we should expect along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says shorter timelines leave less time for algorithmic progress, while longer timelines allow more efficiency gains and lower compute needs. It does not state that shorter timelines assume more efficient algorithms than longer timelines.
